target.thesis: Where output-time facts underdetermine whether a remark was an assertion (blurts, confabulations, and possibly chatbot outputs), the speaker's later owning or disowning helps settle which act was performed. Determinate cases are fixed at utterance.
target.headline: Whether a chatbot output is an assertion is not settled at the time of output by the system's states or functions; it is conferred by what the system later does with the output, so the same token string can be an assertion or a non-assertion depending on its continuation.
target.target: The shared synchronic assumption in Williams and Bayne, Gubelmann, and Butlin and Viebahn that speech-act status depends on states of the producer at the time of output.
target.sketch: Every position in the debate, including Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion, treats speech-act status as a synchronic property fixed by the producer at the moment of production. Intentions, descriptive function, sanctionability and proxy relations are all evaluated at output time. The counterexample is the human case of retroactive ownership. A speaker blurts out a claim without having formed any intention to commit, such as a half-conscious remark or a confabulated explanation. Challenged, they say 'yes, I stand by that', defend it, and retract it when refuted. We rightly say they asserted it, and that they were answerable for it from the start. So the premise that the act is fixed by pre-utterance mental or functional states is false even for humans. Commitment-management after the fact (defending, retracting, updating on challenge) is at least partly constitutive. On this picture the proto-assertion question becomes diachronic and testable. In a long-context or agentic loop, a model that defends, corrects or retracts an earlier output under challenge confers assertoric status on that output, and a one-shot completion never does. The key premise is that retroactive ownership is constitutive of the act rather than merely evidence of an earlier intention.

findings.part: Commitment-management after the fact (defending, retracting) as what assertion is about. The thesis would apply this to the question of which act was performed.
findings.source: Rescorla, "Assertion and its Constitutive Norms", Philosophy and Phenomenological Research, 2009
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="53-6">On the non-restrictive dialectical view, constitutive assertoric norms constrain how one must react if challenged, but do not constrain what one should assert in the first place.</cite> The SEP entry reports the same view: <cite index="48-11,48-12">no norm governs the making of assertions, only norms that govern later reactions.</cite>
findings.note: Later reaction to challenge is made central to assertion, but I saw nothing saying it settles whether an underdetermined utterance was an assertion, and nothing on blurts, confabulation or chatbots, so this is FRAMEWORK and not ENDORSED.

findings.part: The commitment and retraction literature. Its standard direction of explanation is that asserting generates the commitment to defend or retract. The thesis's key premise reverses this.
findings.source: Shapiro, "Commitment Accounts of Assertion" (Oxford Handbook of Assertion chapter, draft); SEP "Assertion" §6.1 on commitment and MacFarlane's retraction rule
findings.what_they_say: The dialectical-norm formulation says that a speaker who asserts that p <cite index="50-11">makes it the case, for as long as S doesn't retract her assertion,</cite> that she is obliged to respond to appropriate challenges. On this ordering, commitment follows from the assertion. The SEP adds that <cite index="31-8">assertion is partly characterized by a commitment to retract the assertion in later adverse contexts.</cite>
findings.note: This is the rival direction of explanation (assertion first, then commitment). I did not see it argued that this ordering cannot be reversed, so it is a rival to answer and not a foreclosure.

findings.part: The claim that later owning or disowning helps settle whether a blurt was an assertion. Also the claim that this reflects constitution and not just evidence.
findings.source: Moran, "Getting Told and Being Believed", Philosophers' Imprint, 2005
findings.what_they_say: Moran treats blurting as still an act of the speaker, and notes that <cite index="64-3,64-4">speaker and audience relate to blurting differently from sleep-talk: the speaker regrets it or tries to make amends.</cite> He concludes that <cite index="64-10">what settles the status of the utterance is whether or not the speaker is presenting it as true.</cite>
findings.note: This is the closest treatment of blurts I found. The speaker's later response is treated as confirming what the utterance was, while presentation at utterance settles it. That is the 'evidence of an earlier state' reading the thesis must rule out. It is a rival and does not conclusively close the claim off.

findings.part: Named target: Williams and Bayne. Their proto-assertion category, and their treatment of the chatbot's commitment-handling.
findings.source: Williams & Bayne, "Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion", Inquiry 69(6), 2026 (arXiv 2410.16645)
findings.what_they_say: The abstract says that, <cite index="4-5">reflecting on the ontogenesis of assertion, they argue for a category of proto-assertion.</cite> The paper holds that <cite index="52-5">a (putative) speaker is capable of assertion only if they stand in the appropriate relation to its governing norms.</cite> A secondary report says they argue chatbots <cite index="8-5">do not treat claims as binding, ensure consistency, or update rationally on new information.</cite>
findings.note: The framing is capacity-based (a speaker's standing relation to norms), with dispositional features such as updating, and not act-level ratification. Compatible with the target ascription but not an explicit synchronic thesis. I did not see the full text, and the secondary report on updating is not verified against it.

findings.part: Named target: Butlin and Viebahn. Whether their requirements are really 'output-time states of the producer'.
findings.what_they_say: They <cite index="11-3">argue an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and be capable of being sanctioned by agents it interacts with.</cite> The second requirement <cite index="11-4">arises from assertion's nature as a norm-governed social practice.</cite>
findings.note: Both requirements concern the system or entity (a function and a standing capacity to be sanctioned). Sanctionability is inherently about later responses, so 'synchronic, fixed at output' is only partly accurate and the thesis should state how it differs. I saw only the abstract.

findings.part: Named target: Gubelmann. The ascription of an intention-at-production view.
findings.source: Gubelmann, "Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case", Philosophy & Technology 37, 2024
findings.what_they_say: The argument is that <cite index="24-5,24-6">using language means acting, but LLMs cannot act because they lack intentions.</cite>
findings.note: This confirms that speech-act status is grounded in producer-side intention. It supports the target ascription for Gubelmann and does not discuss retroactive ownership as far as the abstract shows.

findings.part: Recent work that loosens the producer-state assumption by locating assertoric status in uptake or practice. Possible overlap with the thesis's anti-synchronic motivation.
findings.source: "Assertion, Accountability, and Large Language Models", Philosophy & Technology, 2026; "Who asserts when no one asserts?", Synthese, 2026
findings.what_they_say: The first says <cite index="22-3">the assumption that assertions must be grounded in the properties of individual speakers does not hold uniformly where outputs come from non-agentive systems but are taken up within human practices.</cite> The second <cite index="7-3">introduces a non-psychological functionalist conception of assertion.</cite>
findings.note: These reject producer-state grounding, but via human uptake and function, not the producer's own later owning of a specific output. I saw only snippets, so whether either develops a diachronic ownership account is undecided. Check the full texts before submission.

findings.part: Dialogical tests for whether an utterance is an assertion.
findings.source: Marsili, "The definition of assertion: Commitment and truth", Mind & Language, 2024
findings.what_they_say: Marsili says the speaker is expected to defend the claim against legitimate challenges or else take it back. <cite index="37-2">Only if there is no legitimate way to challenge an utterance can we infer it is not an assertion.</cite>
findings.note: This uses challenge-responsiveness as a diagnostic of assertion, but as an inference from the utterance's challengeability and not from how this speaker later responds. It is related but does not make owning constitutive.

findings.part: Empirical grounding for the human case. People defend confabulated explanations of choices they never made, and tend to take ownership of them.
findings.source: Johansson and colleagues' choice-blindness studies, as reported in e.g. "Manipulation Detection and Preference Alterations in a Choice Blindness Paradigm", PLoS ONE (PMC4172758), 2014
findings.what_they_say: In choice-blindness work, <cite index="42-1">individuals often fail to notice the swap, confabulate explanations for the unselected option, and show increased preference for it.</cite>
findings.note: This is evidence that post hoc owning of confabulation is real and can change the owner's state. It does not address speech-act classification. It is usable as a base for the confabulation case, and also shows owning can reshape the mental state (which a referee may use to argue for the 'evidence of intention' reading).

findings.part: Testability of the diachronic proposal for LLMs. Retraction under challenge in a conversation can be measured.
findings.what_they_say: The authors investigate <cite index="72-1">how models retract high-confidence claims under structured pressure within a single conversation.</cite> They report <cite index="72-3">all tested models eventually abandoned well-established truths under sustained adversarial pressure.</cite>
findings.note: It shows that defence and retraction behaviour in long contexts is measurable, which fits the 'diachronic and testable' step. It is an empirical preprint and does not use the assertion framework.

credit: Rescorla 2009 — assertoric norms govern reactions to challenge (defend or retract), not the making of the assertion
Moran 2005 — blurting is still an act of the speaker, and the speaker's later regret or amends marks the difference from mere mechanical production
Williams & Bayne 2024/2026 — graded proto-assertion, and the point that chatbots' handling of commitment and updating is relevant to assertion
Butlin & Viebahn 2025 — sanctionability by interlocutors as a requirement on assertion
Gubelmann 2024 — the intention-based view of speech acts that the thesis opposes
MacFarlane and the commitment-account literature (SEP; Shapiro) — retraction and defence as the core of assertoric commitment
finding.not_found: No source I found argues that a speaker's later owning or disowning is constitutive of (and not just evidence for) whether an underdetermined utterance, such as a blurt or confabulation, was an assertion. No source applies this to chatbot assertion or to long-context or agentic retraction. So nothing met the ANTICIPATED standard, but this is weak evidence given what I could not see. I saw only abstracts or snippets of Williams & Bayne, Butlin & Viebahn, Gubelmann, Moran, Marsili, Rescorla and the two 2026 LLM-assertion papers, and no full texts. I did not search the philosophy of action literature on after-the-fact ratification or adoption of actions, nor the legal literature on ratification. I did not search the philosophy of mind on confabulation and ownership of attitudes (e.g. Schwitzgebel on post hoc self-interpretation), nor linguistics or conversation-analysis work on repair and self-correction. I also did not search for empirical work on how people judge speech acts retrospectively. The only empirical searches were choice blindness and LLM retraction. The first was not about speech acts, and the second was not about assertion. Whether Williams & Bayne's full text says anything about persistence or retraction of particular outputs is unverified.

sep.why: The theses concern what makes an utterance an assertion (and whether chatbot outputs or blurts qualify), which the assertion entry covers directly, with speech-acts as the neighbouring debate on speech-act status and commitment; the artificial-intelligence entry is the closest available fit for the chatbot angle.

findings.position: Commitment accounts: asserting commits the speaker to respond to challenges or retract, with later conduct (defending or retracting) as the consequence of asserting. The entry treats this as following from the act, not as fixing which act was performed.
findings.who: Brandom, MacFarlane, Peirce, Alston, Green, Rescorla
findings.quote: making an assertion commits you to respond to people's questions and challenges in certain ways, as the conversation evolves.
findings.note: Later owning/disowning is tied to assertion, but as a consequence of the act, not a determinant of what act occurred.

findings.position: Austin's uptake condition makes the illocutionary act depend on the hearer's understanding. The entry says this is implausible for speaker-content verbs like 'assert', which suggests the act is settled at utterance by speaker-side facts.
findings.quote: Bill still asserted that it was closed, since Bill believed she was still there.
findings.note: Supports fixing the act at utterance, but concerns hearer uptake, not later speaker ownership.

findings.position: Rescorla holds there is no norm on making assertions, only norms governing later reactions: defend or retract when challenged. This puts weight on post-utterance conduct, though for norms, not for act-identity.
findings.quote: argues there is no norm at all for proper making of assertions. There are only norms that govern later reactions.
findings.note: Nearest view that makes later conduct central, but it does not use that conduct to settle which act was performed.

findings.position: Indeterminacy of force or content: some hold that an utterance fails to be assertoric when intended content or force is not determinate to the hearer. Others object. This is the entry's one discussion of underdetermined cases.
findings.who: Fricker (2012); objections by Hawthorne, Peet, García-Carpintero
findings.quote: as soon as it is not fully determinate to the hearer what the intended content of an utterance is, or what force it is made with, the utterance fails to be assertoric.
findings.note: Gives the thesis its underdetermination problem, but the entry's resolution is non-assertion, not later ownership.

findings.position: Sneaky and indirect assertions, and the dispute over whether an utterance is an assertion proper, show that act-identity is contested where the literal content differs from what is asserted.
findings.quote: One question is whether an utterance is an assertion proper that p if that content is not exactly what is expressed, or whether it is an act of a related kind
findings.note: Related borderline-act problem, resolved without appeal to later owning.

findings.position: Mere self-commitment is not sufficient for asserting: Pagin's counterexample (37) puts pressure on hearer-directed and commitment views. A thesis that makes later owning help settle act-identity must answer it.
findings.who: Pagin (2004); Pegan, MacFarlane, García-Carpintero, Marsili & Green
findings.quote: incurring a commitment is not sufficient for asserting.
findings.note: Rival to any ownership-based criterion, though the thesis only claims that owning 'helps settle' the act in indeterminate cases.

nearest_positions: Commitment accounts: the assertor is accountable and must defend or retract in response to challenge — Brandom, MacFarlane, Peirce, Alston, Green
Rescorla: no norm on making assertions, only on later reactions (defend or retract)
Austin's uptake and the speaker-side view of 'assert' — the act is fixed by speaker-side facts at utterance
Fricker vs Hawthorne, Peet, García-Carpintero: indeterminate force or content and whether it blocks assertion
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: The entry does not discuss blurts, confabulations, or chatbot outputs. It also does not discuss whether a speaker's retrospective owning or disowning helps determine which speech act an underdetermined utterance was. It says nothing on a split between determinate cases fixed at utterance and indeterminate cases settled afterwards.

findings.position: A speech act, once performed, can later be retracted or withdrawn. The entry stresses that retraction does not change the fact that the act was performed. This is the closest the entry comes to later speaker conduct bearing on an act, but it treats the later conduct as discharging commitments from an already-fixed act, not as settling which act it was.
findings.who: Sbisà 2007, as reported by Green (the entry's author)
findings.quote: nothing I can do on Wednesday can change the fact that I made a promise or assertion on Monday. However, on Wednesday I may be able to retract a claim I made on Monday.
findings.note: Retraction presupposes a determinate act at utterance time. A referee will use it to say that later disowning withdraws an assertion and does not fix its identity.

findings.position: Whether some acts are performed at all can depend on later audience uptake. A bet is not made unless the addressee accepts it. This is an event after the utterance that settles whether a speech act occurred, but it concerns the addressee's response, not the speaker's later owning or disowning.
findings.quote: I cannot bet you $100 on who will win the election unless you accept that bet. If you do not accept that bet, then I have tried to bet but have not succeeded in betting.
findings.note: A structural precedent for post-utterance factors affecting act identity. It is hearer-side and applies only to uptake-requiring acts.

findings.position: On the intentionalist/overtness view, whether an act is an assertion is fixed by what the speaker overtly manifested at utterance, namely commitment to defend the content against 'How do you know?' challenges. Later conduct does not enter. Nothing in the entry makes the act's identity depend on later ratification.
findings.who: Strawson 1964; Green 2013, 2019 (the entry's author's own view)
findings.quote: speech acts involve intentional undertaking of a publicly accessible commitment; further, that commitment is not undertaken simply by virtue of my intending to undertake it
findings.note: This is the rival to answer. If the speaker's overt manifestation at utterance fixes the act, later owning is at most evidence of it. The thesis would need to claim it is partly constitutive for the underdetermined cases.

findings.position: The entry gives the thesis its premise that output-time facts can underdetermine force. Content and mood underdetermine force, and a true utterance may not be an assertion at all (the microphone test and the somniloquist). Where a speaker's intention is not made manifest, the entry says no indirect act is performed. It also allows that clues and inference to the best explanation can settle an act's identity.
findings.who: Green (the entry's author); Bertolet 1994 on indirect speech acts; Davidson 1979 (autonomy)
findings.quote: Testing a microphone in a windowless room, I utter, "It's raining," and it happens to be raining outside. Here I have said something true but have made no assertion.
findings.note: A basis for the underdetermination premise and for the 'determinate cases fixed at utterance' half. It says nothing about blurts, confabulation or chatbots.

findings.position: Strong illocutionary commitment shows that one can perform a speech act without intending it, by intentionally performing other acts that jointly satisfy its conditions. This is another route to act identity not fixed by the speaker's intention at the time. It is still determined by what was performed at that time.
findings.who: Searle and Vanderveken 1985, as discussed by Green
findings.quote: it is difficult to see how one can perform S n while having no intention of performing a speech act at all.
findings.note: Shows the entry already treats act identity as sometimes outrunning the speaker's occurrent intention. This is fixed by the other acts performed, not by later conduct.

nearest_positions: Intentionalism/overtness: force is fixed by what the speaker overtly manifests at utterance — Strawson 1964; Green 2013, 2019
Retraction as withdrawal of a fixed past act — Sbisà 2007 (as reported by Green)
Uptake-dependence of some acts (Austin's misfires; bets need acceptance) and illocutionary silencing — Austin 1962; Langton 1993; Hornsby and Langton 1998; Bird 2002; Maitra 2009
Force conventionalism: acts are fixed by conventions or constitutive rules in force at utterance — Austin 1962; Searle 1969
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: The entry says nothing about blurts, confabulation, or chatbot or LLM outputs. It does not discuss later owning or disowning by the speaker as settling which act was performed, and it does not discuss speaker-side retrospective determination of act identity. Retraction is treated only as discharging commitments from an already-determinate act.

findings.position: The entry treats AI language ability through the Turing Test, i.e. behavioral/linguistic indistinguishability judged from outputs. It offers no account of which speech act an output performs, and it ties no such status to later owning or disowning.
findings.who: Turing (1950); Nilsson (1998); Descartes (1637) on speech as a test
findings.quote: Passing in this sense operationalizes linguistic indistinguishability.
findings.note: The entry concerns output-based tests of intelligence, not assertion-status. It is a distant neighbour only.

findings.position: The entry says that open-domain question-answering has no agreed formal characterization, and that systems like Watson do not converse or reason on the fly. This bears on whether chatbot outputs could count as assertions at all.
findings.who: The entry's own discussion of Watson, Levesque (2013)
findings.quote: Watson can't converse on the fly.
findings.note: This is background on the limits of machine language use. It says nothing about speech acts.

nearest_positions: Turing Test: linguistic indistinguishability as the criterion for machine thought — Turing 1950, Nilsson 1998
Descartes's speech test: machines cannot arrange speech to reply appropriately to everything said — Descartes 1637
Strong vs. weak AI and the Chinese Room: whether machine outputs involve understanding — Searle, as the entry's section 8 outlines (the text is truncated before it)
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Speech acts, assertion, blurts, confabulation, and the retroactive role of a speaker's owning or disowning in fixing an act's type. The entry also does not discuss whether chatbot outputs are assertions. The thesis lies wholly outside its scope, and the text breaks off before the philosophy-of-AI sections.

theses: Where output-time facts underdetermine whether a remark was an assertion (blurts, confabulations, and possibly chatbot outputs), the speaker's later owning or disowning helps settle which act was performed. Determinate cases are fixed at utterance.
